author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: Trade and investment ministers set the frame at AIM Congress
deck: The UAE's foreign trade minister, Dubai Chambers and the GCC secretariat shared a platform with visiting heads of delegation.
excerpt: AIM Congress closed in Dubai with UAE trade and chamber leadership alongside visiting heads of delegation, under the patronage of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.
content:
AIM Congress closed its fifteenth edition at Dubai World Trade Centre on 9 September, held under the patronage of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum and themed around reshaping global prosperity.

The UAE's own representation was senior and trade-focused. Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi attended as Minister of State for Foreign Trade, alongside Mohammad Ali Rashed Lootah, president and chief executive of Dubai Chambers, and Jasem Al-Budaiwi, Secretary General of the Gulf Cooperation Council. Sheikh Saud bin Saqr Al Qasimi, UAE Supreme Council member and Ruler of Ras Al Khaimah, was among the heads of delegation, promoting an emirate hosting more than 73,000 registered companies.

That combination — a trade minister, a chamber of commerce and the GCC secretariat — describes the congress's function accurately. It is an investment promotion event, and the parties on the platform are the ones responsible for the frameworks within which cross-border investment happens: trade agreements, company registration, dispute resolution and the regional coordination the GCC provides.

Dubai Chambers occupies a particular position in that arrangement. It registers and represents companies operating in the emirate, runs international representative offices, and functions as the practical route by which a foreign business establishes locally. For visiting delegations seeking to attract UAE investment, it is also the counterparty that can identify which of its members might supply it.

The GCC's presence reflects a wider point about how Gulf investment reaches external markets. Capital deployed from the region increasingly moves through structures spanning more than one member state, and the regulatory harmonisation the secretariat pursues determines how straightforward that is.

The substantive material for a physical-economy readership came from the congress's Africa sessions, where the UAE's $110bn of investment into African projects between 2019 and 2023 — more than $70bn of it into green energy and renewables — was set alongside Ethiopia's stated 60,000 megawatt renewable potential and a target of 50,000 megawatts by 2030. Wamkele Mene, Secretary-General of the African Continental Free Trade Area, argued for building refining and manufacturing capacity rather than exporting raw commodities.

Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar Properties, and Salman Mahdi of Deutsche Bank's private bank spoke from the investment side. The Kyrgyz Republic presented its Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory as a Central Asian gateway.

Audited attendance figures for the 2026 edition are published by the organiser after the event; pre-show material anticipated more than 20,000 participants and over 400 institutions.

For a construction and industrial readership the useful material at an event of this kind lies in what the investment commitments eventually build. Infrastructure, energy and manufacturing capacity are the destinations for a substantial share of Gulf outbound capital, and the projects that follow are reported as they reach award.
